figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Overview of NanoKV for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. (a) Joint head–channel encoding stores historical KV as coefficients and shared centers, read through full-dimensional (NanoKV) or mixed-dimensional (NanoKV-Fast) decoding and attention. (b) The encoder compresses residuals into INT4 coefficients; the decoder reconstructs them and adds back centers. (c) Key decoders use block-output alignment; Value encoders and decoders use quantization-aware fitting. (d) A fixed policy routes history to full- or low-dimensional attention. The latter reduces Queries and restores output dimensions before LSE merging.

Motivated by the cross-head redundancy in Section 3, we concatenate each token’s $H$ heads with $D$ channels into $x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{HD}$ and compress them jointly, without removing tokens (Figure 4(b)).

abstract: Autoregressive video models rely on historical key–value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over extended rollouts, making KV storage and repeated attention over history a growing memory and computational bottleneck. Aggressive compression can degrade generation quality, while reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention computation largely unchanged. We introduce NanoKV, a frozen-backbone framework for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. NanoKV exploits redundancy across tokens and attention heads by storing shared content in cluster centers and encoding joint head–channel residuals into low-bit coefficients. Crucially, NanoKV uses different fitting objectives for Keys and Values according to their distinct roles in attention: Key decoders are optimized to preserve downstream block outputs, whereas Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. Building on the same compressed representation, the optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention, reducing computation without modifying the video backbone. Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV consistently improves the quality–storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV achieves $26.09\times$ effective KV compression—nearly twice that of KVTC—while improving PSNR by 1.0 dB. NanoKV-Fast retains $20.53\times$ effective compression and achieves an approximately $1.15\times$ end-to-end speedup over KVTC.

sections.body: The section says autoregressive video models keep historical key–value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over long rollouts, so storage and attention over history grow with rollout length. Discarding history removes scene information, and reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention cost largely unchanged. The authors argue compression should preserve the downstream effect on generation, not only reconstruction accuracy. NanoKV freezes the backbone, stores shared cluster centers with joint head–channel residual coefficients, and fits Key decoders by block-output alignment and Value codecs through the deployed quantization path. Optional NanoKV-Fast computes mixed-dimensional attention from the same coefficients. The introduction reports up to $26.09\times$ effective KV compression across three backbones.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Growing KV history raises memory and attention costs, so NanoKV compresses historical KV while preserving downstream generation.

sections.body: Related work falls into three groups. Token-selection methods keep only parts of the history, such as TempCache, WorldKV and Sparse Forcing; NanoKV keeps the history policy and compresses the retained features instead. Feature-compression methods use quantization or low-rank projection, including QVG and KVTC, and the authors adapt KVTC as their primary feature-compression baseline. Computation-reduction work includes VideoMLA, which modifies KV projections and adapts the model for latent-space attention, and sparse video attention, which limits Query–Key interactions. The section distinguishes NanoKV-Fast, which builds mixed-dimensional KV from compressed coefficients while keeping the backbone frozen.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work selects history tokens, compresses features, or changes the model; NanoKV compresses retained features with a frozen backbone.

sections.body: The section motivates three design choices. For redundancy, it compares spatial, spatiotemporal, per-head channel, and joint head–channel PCA at the same $8\times$ dimensional budget; joint compression retains 93.7% of Key variance and 93.1% of Value variance. Because compression errors propagate through Transformer blocks, the authors approximate the Key discrepancy as $\delta_{\ell+1}\approx J_{\ell}\delta_{\ell}+\epsilon_{\ell}$, where $J_{\ell}$ is the local block Jacobian. Figure 3(b) shows output error growing with depth, and block-output alignment reduces the mean error by 15.3%. The section notes that retained variance alone does not establish fidelity to downstream generation. The third question is whether the compact state can also reduce attention computation, which motivates mixed-dimensional attention.
sections.heading: Motivation
sections.headline: Joint head–channel compression retains the most KV variance, and Key block-output alignment reduces mean output error by 15.3%.

sections.body: NanoKV concatenates each token's heads and channels and clusters each historical segment with online K-means. Each token stores a center index and a residual relative to its shared center. The encoder maps residuals to $r$ coefficients, which are quantized to INT4 with token-wise scales, and the decoder reconstructs full-dimensional features for attention. Key decoders are trained by layer-group block-output alignment while the encoder stays fixed. Value encoders and decoders are trained with INT4 rounding in the forward pass, so the fit matches the deployed quantization path. NanoKV-Fast builds lower-dimensional decoders for selected heads and merges full- and low-dimensional branches with log-sum-exp statistics. A fixed per-model protection policy routes sensitive layers, heads, and history to higher dimensions.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: NanoKV stores shared centers and low-bit residual coefficients, fitting Key decoders by block-output alignment and Value codecs through quantization.

sections.body: The evaluation covers three frozen backbones, using 100 VBench-I2V images with four camera actions each, or 400 videos per configuration. Fidelity metrics compare against matched Original rollouts, not ground-truth videos. On HY-WorldPlay at nominal 32×, NanoKV reaches 19.56 PSNR and 26.09× KV compression, and NanoKV-Fast reaches 20.53× with a 1.06× speedup. On Matrix-Game 3.5, NanoKV and KVTC have comparable PSNR (19.08 and 18.83), but NanoKV compresses more (14.26× against 9.28×). On LingBot-World 2.0, NanoKV-Fast has a 0.98× speedup, so it is slightly slower than Original. At nominal 16× on HY-WorldPlay, the component analysis raises PSNR from 16.38 to 20.20 as components are added.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV reaches 26.09× effective compression and 19.56 PSNR, against 13.50× and 18.56 for KVTC.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the HY-WorldPlay result: 26.09× effective KV compression, and NanoKV-Fast retains 20.53× compression with 19.04 dB PSNR and approximately 1.15× end-to-end speedup over KVTC. The limitations state that codec fitting and low-dimensional attention adaptation are backbone-specific, and that resident operators reduce effective compression, especially for short histories. NanoKV-Fast's low-dimensional approximation may accumulate errors and further degrade quality over long horizons. The ethics statement notes that lower deployment costs may facilitate misuse, including deceptive media and non-consensual content, and that fidelity to an uncompressed rollout is not a measure of content safety. The reproducibility statement commits to releasing the implementation, fitted codec parameters, and evaluation scripts.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: NanoKV improves the quality–storage trade-off across three backbones, but codec fitting and attention adaptation remain backbone-specific.

sections.body: Appendix A keeps keys before positional encoding, which reduces HY-WorldPlay persistent BF16 visual KV from 41.92 to 20.96 GiB, and lists baseline implementations with their resident precisions. Appendix B reports the controlled compression comparison and codec training settings, including two K-means iterations and INT4 coefficients. It also gives the layer-wise error propagation derivation and a block-output diagnostic in which mean error falls from 0.2667 to 0.2260. Appendix C covers protection policy and mixed-dimensional attention fitting. Appendix D reports NVML peak memory and runtime. Table 11 separates historical-attention savings from overall visual-attention savings, such as 33.53% for HY-WorldPlay at 16×.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers cache and baseline protocols, codec training and error diagnostics, memory and runtime accounting, and additional quality and example figures.
